en: (Compendium of the Collected Works of Books) Section on Divine Marvels, Part Two, Department of Sectarian Schools, Comprehensive Examination, Volume One:

In the eighth year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Later Han, Prince Ying of Chu offered fine silk to atone for his transgressions; the Emperor issued an edict stating that Ying was a follower of the Yellow Emperor and Laozi.

"Regarding the Buddha: [the Emperor] ordered that [the property] be returned and ransomed to assist in providing the abundant offerings for the *upāsakas* (lay devotees) and *śramaṇas* (monks). According to the *Benji* (Basic Annals) of Emperor Ming in the *Book of the Later Han*, this is not recorded.
However, according to the biography of Prince Ying of Chu: when young, Ying was fond of the ways of the *yīxiá* (wandering knights-errant) and associated with guests;
in his later years, he took pleasure in the studies of the Yellow Emperor and Laozi, and performed Buddhist fasts and sacrifices. In the eighth year of the Yongping era..."
An imperial decree was issued that all those throughout the empire sentenced to death were to redeem their lives by paying a fine of silk.

Ying dispatched the Commandant of the Imperial Secretariat to present thirty bolts of yellow silk and white gauze to the Regional Inspector, saying: "As one who relies upon the protection of the Imperial kin, my transgressions and evils have accumulated.

Joyfully accepting Your Majesty’s great grace, I offer this silk and cloth to redeem my sinful offenses. The Regional Inspector reported this to the throne, and the Emperor replied in a decree: "King of Chu recites the teachings of Huang-Lao..."
In his subtle words, [the Emperor] held the benevolent temples of the Buddha in high esteem. Having purified himself for three months and entered into a covenant with the divine, he asked:

"What cause for suspicion or doubt could there be? There must surely be regret and error [in my previous ways]. Therefore, let the funds for my redemption be used to assist in providing the abundant offerings for the *upāsakas* and *śramaṇas*.

He then issued this decree to all the palace attendants throughout the realm. Subsequently, Ying began to have extensive dealings with Daoist practitioners, even fashioning a golden tortoise and a jade crane inscribed with characters.

[He] took these [omens] to be auspicious signs. In the thirteenth year, a man named Yan Guang plotted with Wang Ping of Yuyang, Yan Zhong, and others to fabricate "divine charts" (*tushu*) containing treasonous schemes.

An investigation was launched, and the authorities reported that Ying had gathered together the wicked and sly, fabricated prophetic charts (*tuchan*), and arbitrarily assigned official ranks, establishing various feudal lords, princes, generals, and officials of the rank of two thousand *shi*. Great...

He acted contrary to the Way and was unfit to rule; we request his execution. The Emperor, out of affection for his kin, could not bring himself to do so, and thus deposed Ying and exiled him to Jing County in Danyang.

In the ninth year of the Yanxi era of Emperor Huan’s reign, Xiang Kai submitted a memorial offering earnest admonition regarding the establishment of shrines for the Buddha and Laozi within the palace precincts;

however, the Emperor would not listen. According to the "Discourse and Eulogy" on the Basic Annals of Emperor Huan in the *Book of the Later Han*, the Emperor adorned the Fanglin Park and conducted [ceremonies there].
In the Palace of Zhuolong, canopies were set up to worship the Buddha and Laozi. According to the *Biography of Xiang Kai*, in the ninth year of the Yanxi era, Kai submitted a memorial stating:
"I have heard that shrines for Huang-Lao and the Buddha have been established within the palace.

This Way is pure and void, valuing non-action (*wuwei*), favoring life and detesting killing, and advocating the reduction of desire and the abandonment of luxury. Yet now, Your Majesty does not abandon your cravings."

If the punishment of killing transgresses the principle of reason and deviates from the Way, how could one possibly attain its blessings? Some say that Laozi entered the Yi and Di regions and became the Buddha (Futu).
The Buddha does not stay under a mulberry tree for more than three nights, desiring not to engender long-lasting affection; this is the height of spiritual refinement.
A celestial deity sent him a beautiful woman, but the Buddha said, "This is merely a leather bag filled with blood," and he did not even look at her.
Because his adherence to the One was such as this, he was able to achieve the Way. Now, Your Majesty’s lustful women and beautiful concubines are the most exquisite in all the world.

"Sweet and rich foods, fine drinks—these exhaust all the flavors of the world. How can you wish to follow the teachings of Huang-Lao? Upon the submission of this memorial, he was immediately summoned to the Department of State Affairs (*Shangshu*) to be interrogated regarding his conduct.
The Minister of State Affairs requested that the Office of the Imperial Scribe (*Sili*) formally adjudicate his crime according to the law; he was then arrested and sent to the Luoyang prison.

The Emperor did not execute him; it was as if the Minister of Justice were deliberating on a criminal sentence. According to the *Western Regions Biography*, Emperor Huan was fond of divine matters and frequently made offerings to the Buddha and Laozi.
Consequently, the common people began to practice these faiths to some extent, and they subsequently grew increasingly widespread.

During the Putong era of Emperor Gaozu of the Liang dynasty, an imperial edict was issued to Yu Chengxian. It was decreed that he, whose learning encompassed both Daoism and Buddhism, should be frequently honored and dispatched by the prefectures and counties. (Note:
This is not recorded in the "Basic Annals" of Emperor Gaozu in the *Book of Liang*. However, according to the biography of Yu Shen, during the Putong era, an edict was issued...)

It was said: "Yu Chengxian’s learning penetrates the teachings of Huang-Lao and encompasses those of Buddhism. He neither competes nor strives for worldly gain, remaining content in this state of withered austerity.

He is capable of calming restlessness and encouraging the common people. Yu Chengxian was appointed as Secretariat Director. The governor and county officials were ordered to frequently offer him respectful invitations, hoping he might humble his will;
it was in this way that they hoped to secure him as a "salt and vinegar" (a metaphor for an indispensable minister). According to the biography of Yu Chengxian, his courtesy name was Zhitong.

He was a native of Yanling in Yingchuan. He had exhaustively mastered the Yuanjing and the Buddhist scriptures, leaving nothing uncomprehended; he was also thoroughly refined in the Nine Schools and the Seven Summaries.
When his commandery appointed him as Director of Merit, he did not accept.

In the fourteenth year of the Taian era of Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty, the Later Ruler ascended the throne. He issued an edict prohibiting all monks, nuns, and Daoist priests who did not conform to the scriptures and precepts.
According to the "Basic Annals of the Later Ruler" in the *Book of Chen*, this occurred in the first month of the fourteenth year of Taian.

In the year Ding-si, he ascended the imperial throne. In the fourth month of summer, on the day Geng-zi, he issued an edict concerning monks, nuns, and Daoist priests who practiced heterodox and left-handed paths not conforming to the scriptures and precepts;
furthermore, regarding vulgar sacrifices among the common people, demonic books, and various strange and marvelous matters, he established detailed regulations to prohibit them all entirely.
Emperor Taizu of the Northern Wei was fond of the teachings of Huang-Lao and also revered the Buddha-dharma. According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Taizu" in the *Weishu*, this is not recorded;

however, according to the "Treatise on Śākyamuni and Laozi," when Emperor Taizu pacified Zhongshan and campaigned through Yan and Zhao, Buddhist temples were encountered in every prefecture and commandery he passed through.
All the śramaṇas and Daoist practitioners were treated with the utmost reverence; the imperial army was strictly forbidden from committing any transgressions against them.

Although the Emperor favored the teachings of Huang-Lao and had perused Buddhist scriptures to some extent, as the empire was newly settled, his war chariots were frequently on the move and affairs of state were still in their infancy.
Consequently, he had not yet established monasteries to invite and accommodate the monastic community; nevertheless, he occasionally sought them out from time to time.

Emperor Taizong followed the legacy of Emperor Taizu and was likewise fond of the teachings of Huang-Lao and Buddhism. According to the *Weishu*, Taizong’s Basic Annals (*Benji*), this is not recorded;

however, according to the "Treatise on Śākyamuni and Laozi" (*Shilaozhi*), upon ascending the throne, Taizong followed the achievements of Taizu and was also fond of Huang-Lao, while further venerating the Buddha-dharma.
He established images throughout the capital and the four quarters, and furthermore ordered the śramaṇas to propagate and guide the people.
Secular Record:
In the fifth year of the Taiping Zhenjun era of Emperor Shizu, the private maintenance of śramaṇas and sorcerers was prohibited. According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Shizu" in the *Wei Shu*:
on the wushen day of the first month in spring of the fifth year of Taiping Zhenjun, an edict was issued stating: "The ignorant masses lack understanding..."
They believe in delusions and demonic heresies, privately maintaining shamans and sorcerers, and hoarding books of prophecies, yin-yang divination, cosmological commentaries, and occult arts.
Furthermore, followers among the *śramaṇas* exploit the empty fabrications of the Western Regions to produce portents and calamities.

This is not the way to unify the administration and transformation of the state, nor to spread pure virtue throughout the world. From the princes and dukes downward, even to the common people, there are those who privately maintain [such practitioners].
Any śramaṇas, sorcerers, or artisans working with gold and silver who are found in private households shall all be sent to the official authorities; no one shall be permitted to harbor them.

This deadline is set for the fifteenth day of the second month of this year. Should they fail to emerge by that time, the sorcerers and śramaṇas shall suffer death, and the masters of the households shall face extermination.
This shall be clearly proclaimed so that all may take notice.

In the sixth year of the Tianbao era of Emperor Xianzu of the Northern Qi, an edict was issued for Daoists to become śramaṇas. According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Xianzu" in the *Beiqi shu*, this is not recorded;
however, according to the *Xu Wenxian Tongkao*, in the sixth year of Tianbao, because the two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism...
The same [situation occurred]. Desiring to eliminate one of the two groups, he assembled scholars from both schools to debate before him.
He then issued an edict that all Daoist practitioners must shave their heads and become śramaṇas; four who refused were executed, whereupon they finally complied with the command.
In the third year of the Tiānhé era of Gāozǔ of the Northern Zhou, the Emperor presided over the Dàdé Hall and assembled śramaṇas and secular scholars to lecture on the *Líjì*.
According to the *Běnjì* (Basic Annals) of Gāozǔ in the *Zhōushū*, on the day of Guīyǒu in the eighth month of autumn in the third year of Tiānhé, the Emperor presided over the Dàdé [Hall].
The Emperor assembled the hundred officials, as well as śramaṇas and Daoist masters, and personally lectured on the *Book of Rites*.

On the *wuchen* day of the second month in spring of the fourth year of the Tiānhé era, the Emperor presided over the Dàdé Palace and convened the hundred officials, Daoists, and śramaṇas to discuss the doctrines of Śākyamuni and Laozi.
According to the *Zhou Shu*, "Basic Annals of the High Ancestor," it says... According to Shen...
He lectured again during the Zhongtian period. Once more, at Ziji Hall, he expounded upon the doctrines of the Three Teachings.
Among those who attended were over two thousand court officials, Confucian scholars, Buddhist monks, and Daoist priests.
In the second year of the Jiande era, the Emperor ascended the throne to expound upon the sequence of the Three Teachings. According to the *Basic Annals of Gaozu* in the *Book of Zhou*:
on the day of Guisi, the twelfth month of winter in the second year of Jiande, he assembled his ministers, śramaṇas, and Daoist practitioners.
The Emperor ascended the high seat and distinguished the precedence of the Three Teachings, establishing Confucianism as the first, Daoism as the second, and Buddhism as the third.
Later, in the third year of the Jiande era, the two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism were first proscribed. According to the "Basic Annals of the High Ancestor" in the *Zhou Shu*:

on the bizi day of the fifth month in the summer of the third year of Jiande, the two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism were first proscribed; all scriptures and images were destroyed, and the śramaṇas were dismissed from their offices.

The Daoist practitioners were all ordered to be returned to the common people. On the *wǔmǎ* day of the sixth month, an imperial edict was issued, stating: "The Ultimate Way is vast and profound; its perfected formation is boundless.
Its substance encompasses both emptiness and existence; its principle reaches the utmost mystery and origin. Yet, once the paths diverged, the tributaries flowed ever further apart.

Purity departed and simplicity dispersed, such that form and spirit fell into discord. Consequently, the three schools of Mohism and the eight schools of Confucianism vied with one another over red and purple, while the nine currents and seven summaries conflicted in their differences."
The proliferation of competing doctrines and the obscuration of the Way through minor achievements have long been prevalent. Without a point of convergence, they vie with one another without ceasing.
It would now be fitting to establish the Tongdao Guan (Observatory of the Universal Way).

All the subtle words of the sages and the canonical teachings of former worthies—the golden rules and jade seals, the secret traces and primordial texts—by which the common people are nurtured and the principles of instruction are supported, should all be widely expounded and unified under a single thread.

"Would it not be fitting for those who play upon small mounds to recognize the lofty majesty of Mount Song and Mount Dai, and for those who dwell among pebbles and gravel to realize the profound clarity of the Bohai Sea?
Thus it is recorded in the *Fozu Tongji*: In the second year of the Jiande era of Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou, the Emperor assembled the monks and issued an imperial decree, saying:
'The Six Classics and the teachings of Confucius are appropriate for the world; yet the True Buddha has no image.'"
They venerate stupas and temples; the foolish believe and comply, exhausting their precious wealth in vain. All such scriptures and images should be destroyed.

Since śramaṇas do not respect the profound kindness of their parents, this is the height of rebellion. How could the laws of the state tolerate this? Let them all return to secular life so they may honor and support their parents through filial piety.
At that time, Dharma Master Huiyuan stepped forward from the assembly and replied with defiance: "If you [judge] by means of physical images..."
"Sentient beings have no affairs [with them], and a state has no blessings [from them]. How can the Seven Temples be considered sentient? The Emperor said:
'The Buddhist scriptures are the laws of foreign lands; therefore, they ought to be abolished. The Seven Temples were established by our predecessors, yet even I do not consider them essential;

I shall abolish them along with the others. The Master said: 'If you claim that because these are the laws of a foreign land, they are not to be used here, then what about that which was spoken by Zhongni (Confucius)?"
"In the lands of Lu, Qin, and Jin, [the rites] likewise should not be practiced. If the Seven Temples are abolished, then the Five Classics will become useless;

if the Three Teachings are all discarded together, by what means can one govern the state? The Emperor said, "Although the territories of Lu, Qin, and Jin differ, they are all none other than the transformation of a single King.
The Master said, "If Qin and Lu share the same royal transformation, then Zhendan (China) and Tianzhu (India) are likewise situated within the realm of Yanmo (Jambudvīpa)."
The Emperor and the Master exchanged views several times, up to twelve rounds; the Emperor could not prevail.
In the fifth month of the third year, the Emperor desired to abolish the Buddhist teachings unilaterally and ordered the Daoist Zhang Bin to compose deceptive rhetoric.
He intended to crush the son of the Śākyas. Master Huiyuan, knowing the Emperor’s intent, responded with vigorous resolve.

Since the Emperor’s guest [the monk] could not be subdued, he immediately displayed his celestial majesty and issued challenging words. His attendants shouted for Huiyuan to listen to the decree, but Huiyuan responded with composure;

his exposition of the principles was so sublime that none of the high-ranking ministers present failed to admire and praise him. Only the Emperor remained displeased. The following day, he issued an edict abolishing Buddhism altogether.
He abolished the two teachings of Daoism and Buddhism, destroyed all scriptures and images, and ordered all śramaṇas and daoshi to return to secular life.
At that time, more than two million monastics and Daoists within the borders of the kingdom reverted to lay dress.
In the first year of the Daxiang era of Emperor Xuan, images of the Buddha and the Celestial Venerable (Tianzun) were first restored.

According to the *Zhou Shu*, in the "Basic Annals of Emperor Xuan," on the *renxu* day of the tenth month in winter of the first year of Daxiang, the Emperor visited Daohui Garden for a great *jiao* sacrifice. He enshrined the High Ancestor, Emperor Wu, as a companion in the sacrifice;
upon its conclusion, they held a doctrinal discussion in the mobile palace (*xingdian*). In this same year, images of the Buddha and the Celestial Venerable were first restored.

The sacred image. At this time, the Emperor sat facing south together with the two images. Various performances were extensively staged, allowing the officials and commoners of the capital to view them at will.

According to the *Fofa jintang bian* (Compendium on the Buddhist Dharma as a Bulwark), during the first year of Emperor Xuan’s Dacheng era, the śramaṇa Daolin had previously presented himself for an audience based on his scholarly attainments;
he engaged in debate with Emperor Wu for twenty days, exchanging views seven times.
Ten times [Dao-lin] petitioned, but Emperor Wu could not be persuaded to yield. He eventually granted permission for the restoration of the teachings.

Upon the death of Emperor Wu, Dao-lin applied with even greater earnestness, and the Emperor consented. He then issued an edict stating: "The late Emperor was deluded by heterodox arguments and deemed the teachings of Śākya and the Way (Buddhism and Daoism) to be of no benefit;

therefore, he abolished them so they were not practiced. However, as these Great Teachings are of vital importance, how could they be fit for dismissal? Thus, they shall now be restored. Thereupon, they flourished once more.
Furthermore, regarding the two teachings (note: in this year, Da Cheng was changed to Da Xiang):
In the second year of the Da Xiang era, Emperor Jing ascended the throne and again practiced the two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism.

According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Jing" in the *Zhou Shu*, on the day Jiwu of the fifth month in the second year of Da Xiang, Emperor Xuan passed away; the Emperor [Jing] entered and resided at the Tiantai Palace. In the sixth month...

On the gengshen day, he again practiced the two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism. He selected those among the former śramaṇas and Daoists who maintained themselves with sincerity and integrity to enter the Way.
According to the *Xu Wénxiàn Tōngkǎo*, Liu [Chihui] remarked: "This was the intention of Yang Jian.
As he was about to harbor other ambitions, he sought blessings through this means."

In the twentieth year of the Kaihuang era of Emperor Gaozu of the Sui dynasty, an edict was issued stating that those who steal or destroy images of Buddhas or Celestial Venerables shall be judged according to the laws for "improper conduct" (*bùdào*);

those who, as śramaṇas or Daoists, damage images of Buddhas or Celestial Venerables shall be judged according to the laws for "heinous rebellion" (*èní*). (According to the *Sui Shu*, Biography of Emperor Gaozu.)

Basic Annals. The twentieth year of the Kaihuang era, the twelfth month, the day of Xinsi. An edict was issued, stating: "The Buddha-dharma is profound and subtle; the Way of the Dao is empty and harmonious.
Both bestow great compassion, delivering and saving all classes of beings. All sentient creatures without exception receive their protection.

Therefore, we carve and cast sacred images and depict their true forms, so that those throughout the land may gaze upon them and thereby express their sincerity and reverence. Should anyone dare to destroy them..."

To steal the images of the Buddha or the Celestial Honored Ones is judged according to the law of sacrilege; for a śramaṇa to destroy a Buddhist image or a daoshi to destroy a Celestial Honored One is judged according to the law of parricide and rebellion.

The Tang dynasty established the Chongyuan Bureau (Chongyuan Shu) to oversee monasteries and observatories. It was charged with managing the affairs of monks, nuns, Daoist priests, and priestesses within these institutions.

According to the *Tangshu*, "Basic Annals of the Official System" (*Bai guan zhi*), the Chongyuan Bureau consisted of one Director (*ling*) of the eighth rank, lower grade, and one Vice-Director (*cheng*) of the same rank.

Class 9, Lower: This office manages the names and numbers of various monasteries in the capital, maintains registers for Daoist practitioners, and oversees matters concerning *zhai* and *jiao* rituals.

Monks from Silla and Japan who enter the court to study and do not return within nine years are entered into the official registers. Daoists, female Daoist adepts (*nüguan*), monks, and nuns must prostrate before the Son of Heaven.
When staying in private residences, they may not exceed three nights; those who remain beyond this limit shall be punished.
The petitions were submitted in succession; no more than seven days elapsed. For those traveling from afar, the provincial and county authorities provided travel provisions.
Throughout the empire, there were one thousand six hundred and eighty-seven Daoist temples, with seven hundred and seventy-six male Daoists and nine hundred and eighty-eight female Daoists (nüguan).
There were five thousand three hundred and fifty-eight Buddhist monasteries, with seventy-five thousand five hundred and twenty-four monks and fifty thousand five hundred [nuns].
176. Regarding the ordination of monks, nuns, *daoshi*, and *nüguan* in the two capitals, one Censor shall preside over them. Every three years, the prefectures and counties shall compile registers;
one copy shall be retained at the county, and one at the prefecture. One copy of the register for monks and nuns shall be submitted to the Sacrificial Department (*Sicibu*);

one copy for *daoshi* and *nüguan* shall be submitted to the House of the Imperial Clan (*Zongzheng*), and one to the Department of Official Titles (*Sifeng*). Furthermore, there are two officials at the [central] office.
There were three Historians (Shi), six Ritual Officers (Dianshi), and two Custodians (Zhanggu). There was one Doctor of the Chongyuan Academy and one hundred students.

During the Sui dynasty, the office was subordinated to the Ministry of Rites (Honglu). There were also Daoist temples (Daochang) and Yuan-altars (Yuantan). During the Tang dynasty, supervisors were established for the various monasteries and observatories.

They were subordinate to the Court of State Ceremonial (Honglu Si). Each temple and monastery had one supervisor (jian). During the Zhenguan era, the supervisors of temples and monasteries were abolished.
In the second year of the Shangyuan era, the Lacquer Garden Supervisor (Qiyuan Jian) was established, but it was subsequently abolished.
In the Wude era of the Gaozu, he visited the National Academy and commanded the monks and Daoists to lecture on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the *Laozi*.
[Note: This is not recorded in the "Basic Annals of the Gaozu" in the *Jiu Tangshu*.

According to the *Dad Tang Xin Yu*, the Gaozu once visited the National Academy and commanded Xu Wen'uan to lecture on the *Xiaojing*, while the monk Huicheng lectured on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the Daoist Liu Jinjia [lectured on the *Laozi*].]
He was lecturing on the *Laozi* when the Emperor summoned Jian Deming to debate with him. Thereupon, their challenges and refutations arose like a rising tide, and all three were defeated.
The High Ancestor said, "The doctrines of Confucianism, Daoism, and Buddhism each have their own fundamental tenets. Liu [Jingzhi] and Xu [Hui] are both preeminent talents of the present age."
Tademing comprehended it all at once; he may truly be called one who has mastered learning. He was granted fifty bolts of silk.
In the ninth year of Wude, the teachings of the Buddha and Laozi were abolished, but they were soon restored. According to the "Basic Annals of Gaozu" in the *Jiu Tangshu*:
on the xinsi day of the fourth month in the ninth year of Wude, the [teachings of] the Buddha and the Way of Laozi were abolished; on the gengshen day of the sixth month, they were suspended.

Regarding the teachings of the Buddha and Laozi: According to the "Basic Annals of the High Ancestor" (*Gaozu benji*) in the *Old Book of Tang* (*Jiu Tangshu*), on the *xinsi* day of the fifth month in the summer of the ninth year, because the temples and monasteries in the capital were no longer fit for purity, an edict was issued stating: "Śākyamuni expounded the teachings with purity as his priority;
he remained far removed from dust and defilement and severed all greed and desire. It is for this reason that he propagated sublime deeds and cultivated the roots of goodness. [The edict] opened...
To guide the ignorant and deluded, and to serve as a bridge for the common people, he thus expounded the scriptural teachings and disciplined his disciples.
They practiced repentance to harmonize body and mind, renouncing all defiled attachments. Their clothing and food were entirely provided by the fourfold assembly.

Since the Self-Awakened King passed away and the Semblance Dharma began to circulate, the final age has declined, gradually becoming deficient and corrupt. Consequently, there have been those of vulgar and lowly character who schemed to exalt themselves.
Those who are idle and indolent, seeking merely to evade corvée labor and taxes, falsely undergo tonsure and take refuge under the pretext of leaving the household life.
Yet their cravings for desire are insatiable and their pursuits never cease; they frequent villages and dwell among the marketplace crowds, managing landed estates and amassing goods and wealth.

They make their living through farming and weaving, and establish their careers through trade and peddling; their affairs are identical to those of common households, and their conduct is no different from that of ordinary citizens.

Consequently, they advance against the texts of the precepts and retreat from the instructions of the ritual classics. They even personally engage in robbery and plunder, commit burglary themselves, propagate false and heretical doctrines, and conspire with the powerful and the depraved.
Thus, they are constantly ensnared by the legal net and cast themselves into severe punishment, defiling the True Suchness and bringing ruin upon the Dharma.
The Sublime Dharma is like weeds and tares that defile fine grain, or like silt that muddies clear water.
Furthermore, the grounds of the *saṃghārāma* were originally the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*), places for the mind to dwell in tranquility; by principle, they should be secluded and still.

Yet in recent times, many temples and residences have been established there, seeking not spacious and open environments, but merely rushing toward places of clamor and confusion. They construct and gather materials on rugged terrain, raising their rafters...
The layout is disordered and obscured; it harbors the wicked and depraved. Some even adjoin or border upon courtesans' quarters and butcher shops;
dust fills the rooms and the stench of meat and wine overflows the streets. This only serves to foster a spirit of contempt and violates the principles of veneration and respect.

Furthermore, the teachings bequeathed by Laozi were fundamentally rooted in profound emptiness; he cultivated his will through non-action and withdrew his sentiments from the mundane world to preserve his true nature.

To guard the One is called the Primordial Gate. To be driven by worldly affairs is to deviate from this fundamental principle. Having received the mandate to rule the realm, I have sought to cause the teachings to flourish;

my resolve lies in benefiting others, and my heart is set on protection and preservation. I desire to distinguish between jade and stone, and to discern between the fragrant ruan grass and the foul yu grass, so that the wondrous Way may endure forever and the field of merit remain eternally firm.
To rectify the root and clarify the source, it is appropriate to conduct a purge of the various monks and nuns.
As for the Daoist priests and female clerics (*niguàn*), those who are diligent in their practice and observe the precepts shall all be accommodated in major monasteries and cloisters;

they shall be provided with food and clothing so as not to suffer from want. Those who are unable to be diligent in their observance of the precepts, or who are deficient and incapable of receiving offerings, shall all be dismissed and sent back to their native homes.
The relevant authorities shall clearly establish regulations and rules, ensuring that these matters are strictly observed.
Regarding the Buddhist teachings and matters that contravene the regulations, it was deemed appropriate to suspend them all.

Three monasteries were to be retained in the capital, two observatories, and one monastery each in the remaining provinces throughout the empire; all others were to be abolished. However, these measures were ultimately not carried out.

The edict of the fifth year of the Zhenguan era of Emperor Taizong [stated]: "Monks and Daoists shall prostrate before their parents. According to the *Taizong benji* (Basic Annals of Taizong) in the *Jiu Tangshu*, this is not recorded;
however, according to the *Xu Wenxian Tongkao* (Continued Comprehensive Examination of Literary Contributions), it says [as follows].

In the second year of the Longshuo era of Gaozong, an imperial edict was issued [requiring] that Buddhists and Daoists prostrate before the sovereign and their parents. Following the deliberation of Liufu Dechen, another edict was issued [stating] they need not prostrate.
According to the *Jiu Tang Shu*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Gaozu," this is not recorded.

According to the *Jiu Tang Shu*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Gaozong," on the day of Yichou in the sixth month of the second year of Longshuo, it was first ordered that monks, nuns, and others must all perform full prostrations according to the rites.
Regarding their parents: according to the *Fofa jintang bian* (The Buddhist Dharma as a Golden Bulwark), during the early Wude era, Liu Deqin served as Director of the Secretariat.

In the second year of the Longshuo era of Emperor Gaozong, an imperial edict was issued requiring Buddhists and Daoists to prostrate before their sovereigns and parents; the various ministers were then commanded to deliberate upon this matter.

At that time, De-fen served as the Grand Director of the Office of Imperial Preceptors (Sichengguan). He proposed this deliberation: "I humbly submit that the two teachings of Śākyamuni and Laozi possess a profound and vast compassion and reverence.

Because our state has followed these traditions for generations, their veneration has long been established. However, it is necessary to follow their respective principles; it would be inappropriate to require prostrations. Why?
Because shaving the head differs from the ritual of wearing caps and sashes, and holding an alms bowl is not the same as using sacrificial vessels and stands."

In these rites, one extends grace while praying for concentration and wisdom; there is no need for prostrations and kneeling before one’s venerable parents. The Daoist Master [Falu] sent a letter to the provincial ministries, stating: "Since the Great Dharma was spread to the East more than a thousand years ago, its rise and fall have followed the times."
At times, they may briefly fall into distress before eventually rising again; yet nothing has ever been as utterly suppressed and debased as it is today.

Since the middle years of the Shaoxing era, monks and Daoists have been exempted from the poll tax (*dingqian*), with rates ranging from ten thousand coins for the highest to one thousand three hundred for the lowest.

Among the four classes of the state’s subjects—the scholar, the farmer, the artisan, and the merchant—monks and Daoists were formerly registered in the official records and the rolls of officeholders, thereby attaining a status equal to that of the Confucian literati.

The basis for their establishment does not differ from those who govern the state and manage the people; it is simply because they take the Great Sage as their ancestor and transmit his transformative teachings of goodness.
As for the prevalence of celestial calamities and the irregularity of rain and sunshine, they command their disciples to offer prayers on their behalf.
Thus, Heaven and Earth respond and the spirits accord; moreover, this is something that the ears and eyes of the past and present have constantly heard and seen.
If one truly governs the state to ward off calamities and bring forth blessings and auspiciousness, it is only fitting that they should differ somewhat from the common masses.
Why do you so hastily impose a tax on the people that is several times the original amount?

At present, the tax on able-bodied men throughout the world mostly amounts to no more than three hundred strings of cash. Yet, those whose lands are poor or whose labor is arduous often escape this by becoming monks;

conversely, they fail to be ranked among the common people because they neither plow nor weave, yet live off the world for their clothing and food. Now, as for those who plow to eat and raise silkworms...
Furthermore, it was not necessarily the case that everyone outside the monastic community both plowed and raised silkworms (as detailed in the source).
On the first day of the ninth month of the twenty-first year of the Xiangsheng era, the *wuxu* day, temple and monastery properties were confiscated to provide for the academies;
this is recorded in the "Basic Annals of Emperor Gaozong" of the *Song Shi* (as detailed in the source).
On the day of Yichou in the second month of the thirty-first year of the Xiangxing era, the sale of ordination certificates for monks and Daoists was resumed.
(As recorded in the *Song Shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Gaozong," etc.)

In the eighth month of the third year of the Qiandao era of Emperor Xiaozong, Sichuan suffered from drought. Four hundred *duce* (monastic ordination certificates) were granted to the Regional Commandant’s Office to prepare for relief efforts.
(As recorded in the *Song Shi*, Basic Annals of Emperor Xiaozong, etc.)
In the fourth year of the Qiandao era, one thousand ordination certificates for monks and Daoists were issued, and the use of Buddhist or Daoist terminology in examination essays was prohibited.

According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Xiaozong" in the *Song Shi*: on the day of Guihai in the fifth month of the fourth year of Qiandao, one thousand ordination certificates for monks and Daoists were issued.
According to the *Fozu Tongji*: in the ninth month of the fourth year of Qiandao, the Emperor addressed the Minister of Rites...

Li Tao wrote in a letter: "The compositions for the civil service examinations must not employ the terminology of Buddhism or Daoism. If one cultivates oneself in the mountain forests, there is no harm to the Way;
however, if such [language] is employed in the examination halls, it may hinder administrative affairs."
On the day of Jiazi in the second month of the seventh year of the Qiandao era, an edict was issued stating that temples and monasteries were not to be exempted from taxes or corvée labor.
(As recorded in the *Song Shi*, Basic Annals of Emperor Xiaozong...)
In the eighth month of the eighth year of the Qiandao era, scholars of the Three Teachings were summoned to assemble at Neiguantang, where they were granted a vegetarian feast.
[This is not recorded in the *Song Shi*, in the Basic Annals of Emperor Xiaozong; however, it is recorded in the *Fozu Tongji* (as follows).]

In the second year of the Chunxi era, the Baiyun Tang seal was bestowed, ordering that all schools and sects throughout the empire must proceed to the Baiyun Tang for public selection and the application of the seal, as verified by the relevant authorities.
According to the *Song Shi* (History of Song), in the Basic Annals of Emperor Xiaozong, this is not recorded;

however, according to the *Fozu Tongji* (General Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), on the third month of the second year of Chunxi, the Imperial carriage visited Shangzhu to burn incense and pay respects to the Great [Buddha].
The Emperor issued an edict to establish the State-Protecting *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* (Golden Light) Dharma-hall and bestowed the seal of Baoyun Hall (*Báiyún Táng*).

He commanded that the various schools of the Three Studies throughout the realm should all proceed to Baoyun Hall to be collectively appointed for service using the seal, and he instructed the relevant authorities to publicize this decree.
In the seventh year of the Chūnxī era, Chan Master Xuedou was summoned to have an audience with the Emperor, and they discussed the similarities and differences among the Three Teachings.

According to the *Basic Annals of Emperor Xiaozong* in the *History of Song*, this is not recorded. However, according to the *Chronicle of the Buddhas and Patriarchs* (*Fozu Tongji*), in the seventh year of the Chūnxī era, the Chan Master Baoyin of Xuedou in Mingzhou was summoned to have an audience.
The Emperor asked: "The sages of the Three Teachings fundamentally share this same principle. The Master [replied]:...
[The disciple] said: "It is like empty space; originally it has no north or south. The Master said: "It is merely that the gateways established differ.

Thus, Confucius established his teaching through the *Zhongyong* (The Doctrine of the Mean). The Master said: 'Without the *Zhongyong*, how could one establish the mundane world? The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:"
"Without destroying the characteristics of the mundane world, one accomplishes the supramundane Dharma.
The Master said, "Those who study nowadays merely observe the words and do not recognize the Master’s mind. The Teacher said, "It is not only students of today;

even at that time, Yanzi was the most complete in embodying [the Way], yet he could only say, 'He seems to be before me,' or 'Suddenly he is behind me,' or 'He stands there as if toweringly distinct. He too had not yet [fully realized it]."
This is sufficient to recognize the Master’s mind. The Master himself also said: "Disciples, do you think that I am concealing anything from you? I conceal nothing from you.
Judging by this, even the disciples of that time did not yet understand the Master’s mind; how much less so can people of today? Zhang Shangying once remarked:
"Only after one has studied Buddhism can one truly understand Confucianism. The Emperor said: "My own thought has always been..."
Having formed this view, the Emperor further asked, "What is the teaching of Laozi and Zhuangzi like? The Master replied, "It may be compared to those of the Hīnayāna within the Buddha-dharma.
Those of the Hīnayāna loathe the body as if it were shackles and abandon wisdom as if it were mixed poison; they seek to transform their bodies through fire."
One enters the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*). This is just as Zhuangzi said: "The body can indeed be made like withered wood;
the mind can indeed be made like dead ashes. Laozi said: "I have a great affliction: it is that I have a body. A follower of the Mahāyāna, however, is not like this;
they do not realize *bodhi* until all sentient beings have been delivered. This is just as Yi Yin said: "I am one among the people of Heaven who has first awakened."
He intended to use this Way to awaken the people. If there were even a single person who did not receive its benefit, it was as if he himself had pushed that person into a ditch.
The Emperor was greatly pleased and, on that very day, issued an edict appointing him to reside at Mount Jing.
On the *xinwei* day of the eighth month in the fourteenth year of the Chunxi era, one hundred *duodie* (ordination certificates) were granted to provide relief for the destitute.
(As recorded in the *Song Shi*, Basic Annals of Emperor Xiaozong... According to the *Yanyi Yimou Lu*, the ordination certificates for monks and Daoists were tested and issued annually;
woodblocks were carved and paper was used for printing. Once the new system was implemented, those who submitted proposals established fixed prices for their issuance.
They were sold at a rate of one hundred and thirty *qian* per document. Nevertheless, an annual fixed quota was established, and the number could not exceed it.
In the seventh month of the first year of the Xīníng era, their sale to the common people began. Initially, no more than three or four thousand people purchased them each year;
by the sixth year of the Yuánfēng era, the limit was set at ten thousand. However, the Kuizhou Circuit Transportation Commission increased the price to...
The price was reduced sequentially from three hundred *qian* to one hundred and ninety *qian*. In the first year of Jianzhong Jingguo, it was increased to two hundred and twenty *qian*.
By the fourth year of Daguan, over thirty thousand sheets were sold annually; however, with old and new stock piling up, the market price among the common people fell to ninety *qian*.
The court, distressed by this inflation, suspended sales for three years and subsequently pursued those who had purchased them in the capital.

In the meantime, it was disparaged and devalued. When the common people throughout the various circuits heard of this, they all vied with one another to lower the prices and sell their certificates in haste;
the price fell to twenty *qian* per certificate. Subsequently, wealthy families stopped buying them, and the price gradually rose again to over one hundred *guan*.

The authorities reported this to the throne, whereupon an imperial decree was issued stating that for those *du-chie* (ordination certificates) already granted, the price should be increased accordingly, and separate official warrants should be issued to await the filling out of the details for six years. Furthermore, an edict was issued.

The paper was changed to *renji* (woven silk). Following the precedent for the rank of *shōshi-rō kōei* (Junior Officer, Cavalier), in the seventh year of the Xuande era, as the number of monks and Daoists throughout the realm exceeded one million, an edict was issued to grant them certificates for five years.
Subsequently, due to the ravages of war, this was suspended and not implemented. After the southward migration [of the court], new laws were established once more;
the quota for ordination certificates (*dokuhyō*) was increased from sixty thousand to one hundred thousand. At the beginning of the Chunxi era, it was further increased.
It reached three hundred *qian*. It was further increased to five hundred *qian*, and again increased to seven hundred *qian*.

However, the court was cautious and parsimonious, not selling them lightly. Often, people would carry money into the Imperial Capital (*Xingdu*) and engage in various efforts before finally obtaining them.
Later, the "Bed-Stopping" (*Tingtà*) decree was established, permitting individuals to increase their purchase by one hundred *qian* for trade. It was increased yet again.

They were made in quantities of eight hundred. In recent years, the distribution has increased significantly; even at the prefectural and commandery levels, prices have been driven down to the point of extinction as they seek to sell them.
(Tushu Jicheng, Shen Yi Dian, Er Shi Bu Hui Kao, Volume I).
(Tushu Jicheng, Shen Yi Dian, Er Shi Bu Hui Kao, Volume II).

In the first year of the Tiande era of Emperor Hailing of the Jin dynasty, the ordination of monks and Daoists was abolished. According to the *Jin shi* (History of Jin), the Basic Annals (*Benji*) do not record this;
however, the *Xu Wenxian Tongkao* (Continued Comprehensive Examination of Literary Contributions) states [as follows]... [etc.]
On the *wuchen* day of the first month of spring in the first year of the Mingchang era of Emperor Zhangzong, an edict was issued prohibiting those who shave their heads to become monks or Daoists.
(As recorded in the *Jin shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Zhangzong," etc.)

On the *renchen* day of the second month in the second year of the Mingchang era, an edict was issued stating that monks, nuns, and Daoist priests were not permitted to enter the residences of imperial princes or officials of the third rank and above.
(As recorded in the *Jin shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Zhangzong," etc.)

In the third year of the Mingchang era, an imperial edict was issued stating that Buddhists and Daoists must prostrate before their parents; the protocols for these ceremonies were to be strictly in accordance with standard custom.

According to the *Jin shi* (History of Jin), in the Basic Annals of Emperor Zhangzong, on the day of Guisi in the third month of the third year of Mingchang, the Shangshu Sheng (Ministry of Revenue) submitted a memorial stating:

"Those who report on current affairs claim that among the followers of Buddhism and Daoism, there are none who prostrate before their parents or relatives. This is the greatest cause of the ruin of social customs. Regarding this matter...

The officials stated: "An imperial edict from the second year of the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty states: 'We have heard that Daoists, female priests (niguǎn), monks, and nuns do not prostrate before their parents.

This is to be a child who forgets the source of their life, showing arrogance toward their kin while pursuing trivial matters. From this day forward, they shall all be permitted to prostrate before their parents.
Regarding mourning periods, their gravity, and the protocols for senior relatives, these shall all conform strictly to standard regulations. We, your servants, [therefore]...
It is appropriate to rely on historical precedents; thus, the regulations for its implementation were established.

In the first year of the Cheng’an era (corresponding to the fifteenth year of the Dading era), an imperial edict was issued stating that monks, nuns, Daoist priests, and priestesses aged sixty and above must all receive ordination.
According to the *Jin shi* (History of Jin), in the sixth month of the first year of the Cheng’an era...

On the day of Dingmao in the month of the moon, an imperial edict was issued: "From now on, for the Grand Masters (Changlao Dashi) and Great Virtuous Monks (Dade), regardless of age, Grand Masters shall be permitted to ordain three disciples and Great Virtuous Monks two.
Monks who have observed the precepts for forty years or more may ordain one.
Furthermore, those registered as *śrāmaṇeras* in the fifteenth year of Dading who are sixty years of age or older shall all be required to receive full ordination."
Furthermore, it was not permitted to ordain disciples, nuns, *daoshi*, or *nüguan*; the same applied to them as well.
In the second year of the Cheng’an era, monastic and Daoist ordination certificates (*duodiep*), purple and brown robes, and titles of clerical virtue were issued to assist in military provisions.

According to the *Jin shi* (History of Jin), Basic Annals of Emperor Zhangzong, in the fourth month of summer in the second year of Cheng’an, the Shangshu Sheng (Ministry of Revenue) memorialized that in recent years, due to the north...

The border regions were in great need of provisions. He requested that monks and Daoists be granted honorary ordination certificates (*du-chie*), purple and brown robes, and titles of venerable masters (*shide hao*) to assist in replenishing the military stores.
The Emperor granted his request.

On the day of Guiyou in the twelfth month of the second year of Taihe, three thousand ordination certificates (jie-die) were granted to monks and Daoists to commemorate the first birthday of the Crown Prince.
(As recorded in the *Jin shu*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Zhangzong," etc.)

In the second year of Xuanzong’s Xingding era, an edict was issued stating that monks and Daoists along the borders were permitted to receive ordination only within their respective localities and were allowed to remain there as before;
those from outside were to be sent to the prefectural gates to have their entries and exits inspected.

According to the *Jin shi* (History of Jin), in the tenth month of winter in the second year of Xingding, on the day of Wu-wu, the Shangshu Sheng (Ministry of Revenue) reported that they had captured spies and fugitives who had defected.

There were many monks and practitioners. An imperial edict was issued to the various prefectures along the borders, stating that ordinations should be granted only within their respective jurisdictions and that they were permitted to remain in their current residences.
However, those who came from north of the Yellow River and east of Mount Tai were sent into the interior provinces, where their entry and exit were strictly monitored.
In the first year of the Yuan Xuanzong era, in the sixth month of summer, the monk Haiyun was appointed to oversee the affairs of Buddhism,
and the Daoist Li Zhenchang was appointed to oversee the affairs of Daoism. (As recorded in the *Yuan Shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Xuanzong," etc.)
In the [X]th year of Emperor Xianzong’s reign, he summoned representatives of both the Buddhist and Daoist traditions to the imperial presence to debate their doctrines.

As the Buddhists prevailed, he issued an edict for the Daoists Fan Zhisheng and others to shave their heads and become monks. According to the *Basic Annals of Emperor Xianzong* in the *History of Yuan*, this is not recorded;

however, according to the *Continued Compendium of Literature and Institutions* (*Xu Wenzhuan Tongkao*), when the Emperor Shizu was still residing at his private residence, Emperor Xianzong issued an imperial decree ordering the two [traditions of] monks and Daoists...
The two families went together to the Emperor to present their case. They made a mutual agreement: "If the Daoists prevail, the monks shall shave their heads and become Daoists;
if the monks prevail, the Daoists shall shave their heads and become monks. Subsequently, the monks prevailed.

The Emperor dispatched the close minister Tuo Huan to lead the Daoist practitioners, including Fan Zhisheng and seventeen others, to Longguang Temple to shave their heads and become monks. [They] burned...

Fifty-four apocryphal scriptures were eliminated. Of the Buddhist temples throughout the empire that had been occupied by Daoist practitioners, two hundred and thirty-seven were all ordered to be returned [to their original religious affiliation].
In the second year of Shizu’s Zhongtong era, monks and Daoists were investigated and surveyed.

According to the *Basic Annals of Shizu* in the *History of Yuan*, in the fifth month of the second year of Zhongtong, Wang You was dispatched to the Sichuan circuits and other regions to investigate monks and Daoists.
In the eighth month, five hundred *qing* of land were granted to Qingshou Temple and Haiyun Temple.

In the third year of Zhongtong, due to celestial portents, an imperial edict was issued to perform Buddhist rites and establish *zhao* (sacrificial altars). According to the *Yuan Shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Shizu":
on the day of Yibyou, the eleventh month of the third year of Zhongtong, Venus (Taibai) invaded the Hook and Bell asterism (Gouling).

On the day of Dinghai, an edict was issued for Sheng'an Temple to perform the *Foding Jinyun* (Buddha’s Crown Golden Wheel) rite, while Changchun Palace established a *Jinlu Zoutian Zhao* (Golden Register Universal Heaven Sacrifice).

On the gengwu day of the fourth month in summer of the third year of Zhizheng, an imperial edict was issued for monks and Daoists to pray for blessings at the temples and observatories in the capital.
On the guichou day of the ninth month in autumn of the fourth year of Zhizheng, the prohibitions against monks, nuns, and Daoist masters were strictly enforced throughout the regions of Xixia,
Zhongxing, and others.
In the seventh year of the Zhizhi era, on the gengzi day of the ninth month, an imperial edict was issued stating that those among the monks, Daoists,
and Yeliqun who had families and did not observe the precepts were to be registered as commoners.

On the day of Guiwei, the seventh month of autumn in the twelfth year of Zhizhen, an edict was issued dispatching envoys to the south of the Yangtze River to search for and interview monks, Daoists, practitioners of Yin-Yang, and others.
On the day of Gengwu, the sixth month of the thirteenth year of Zhizhen, an imperial decree was issued to the monks and Daoists of Xijing, as well as to the Yelükeun and Dashi... [and so forth].
Those among the Mian and other groups who possessed wives and families were treated as one body with the common people and required to pay taxes.

On the *jichou* day of the tenth month in the winter of the nineteenth year of the Zhiyuan era, an imperial edict was issued stating that monks and Daoists of Hexi, as well as Yeliqewens (Yelü Yekeun), who had wives and families, were to pay taxes together with the common people.
(The above is from the *Basic Annals of Emperor Shizu* in the *History of Yuan*, etc.)
In the twenty-fifth year of Zhizhen, an edict was issued to perform Buddhist rites and establish a *zhao* (sacrificial ritual).

According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Shizu" in the *Yuanshi*, in the twelfth month of winter in the twenty-fifth year of Zhizhen, Yi-si-ma and more than seven hundred others were ordered to perform Buddhist rites and observe a period of silent meditation (*zuo jing*) at the Yuta Hall, the Imperial Bedchamber, and various temples including Wanshoushan and Huguo Renwang. In total...
In the fifty-fourth assembly, on the third day of the spring second month in the twenty-seventh year of the Zhizhi era, the Celestial Master Zhang Zongyan held a three-day *zhao* ritual.
There were four hundred and ninety-one monks and Daoist priests from Shunzhou in attendance.
To provide ninety days' worth of grain for those suffering from famine. (As recorded in the *Yuanshi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Shizu" [etcetera]).

In the twenty-ninth year of Zhizhi, on the day of Guihai in the seventh month of autumn, Yeliwailisasha had previously recruited monks, Daoists, Confucians, Yelikeyun, and Dachi-man to serve in the military.
An imperial decree was issued ordering that they cease being enrolled in the military registers. (As recorded in the *Yuan*...)
*History of the Shizu (Emperor Shizu) Basic Annals* (as stated).

In the first year of the Yuanzhen era of Emperor Chengzong, the Jade Gui was bestowed upon the Celestial Master Zhang Yudi and others; furthermore, the Imperial Preceptor was granted a Buddha-crown, and a palace and stupa were constructed for him.
According to the *History of Yuan*, the Basic Annals of Emperor Chengzong, in the second month of spring in the first year of the Yuanzhen era:
The Jade Rulers (*yùguī*) were bestowed upon thirteen individuals, including the Celestial Master Zhang Yudi, the Patriarchal Master Zhang Liusun, and the Perfected Man Zhang Zhixian;
each was crafted from precious jade. A crown of the Five-Direction Buddhas was bestowed upon the Imperial Preceptor (*dìshī*).

In the third month, as the labor for spring cultivation was in full swing, all non-essential construction projects were suspended, with the exception of the Imperial Preceptor’s stupa and the monastery of Dharma Master Zhang.
In the first year of the Dade era, an imperial edict was issued to establish prohibitions and regulations for monks and Daoists. According to the *Basic Annals of Chengzong* in the *Yuanshi*:

In the sixth month of summer in the first year of Dade, an edict was issued stating that monks and Daoists who commit serious crimes such as adultery and theft shall be subject to interrogation by the relevant authorities.

On the *renxu* day of the eleventh month, it was prohibited for monks and Daoists to arbitrarily occupy mining sites, charcoal fields, and mountain ranges. On the *wuxu* day of the twelfth month, the Zhongshu [Shengyuan]...

The provincial ministers, together with the Henan Chancellor Barlan and others, submitted a memorial stating: "Wealthy households evade labor service and taxation by falsely claiming to be monks or Daoists.

Furthermore, these monks and Daoists engage in commerce and maintain wives and children, no different from the common populace. We request that they be stripped of their status and returned to the civilian population."

During the Song dynasty, those who became monks or Daoist priests were first required to pay a fee to the local authorities before being granted ordination certificates (*duòdì*). Today, no fixed regulation exists, and those who seek such status through mere chance must be numerous.
The Emperor ordered that a proposal be drafted and reported to him.
In the sixth year of the Dàdé era, in the eleventh month of winter, an imperial edict was issued to the monasteries and observatories of Jiangnan:
all privately acquired fields and those designated as "donations" by the populace shall have their rents redistributed to fulfill labor service obligations.
In the eighth year of Dade, the fourth month of summer, an edict was issued requiring monks who engaged in trade to pay taxes.
According to the above, these entries are found in the *Basic Annals of Chengzong* in the *History of Yuan* (Yuan Shi). (As stated...)
In the fifth month of the eleventh year of Dade, Emperor Wuzong ascended the throne.

In the twelfth month, an edict was issued stating that monks, Daoists, Yeliqun, and Dasiman were to pay taxes according to the previous regulations. (As recorded in the *Basic Annals of Emperor Wuzong* in the *History of Yuan*, etc.)
In the second year of the Zhida era of Emperor Wuzong, an edict was issued to levy taxes on monks and Daoists. According to the *Basic Annals of Emperor Wuzong* in the *History of Yuan*:

on the day of Yihai in the sixth month of summer in the second year of Zhida, the ministers of the Zhongshu Sheng (Secretariat) reported that the Xuanzheng Yuan (Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs) had submitted a petition to exempt monks, Daoists, Yelikeyun (Muslims), and Dashi-man (Jews) from land taxes. The ministers deliberated upon the matter of the fields...
There are rents; there are taxes on merchants. These are the established laws of our ancestors. Now, the Xuanzheng Yuan has petitioned for a blanket exemption, which is contrary to regulation.
By imperial decree, they shall be collected according to the old system.
In the fourth year of the Zhida era, Renzong ascended the throne and abolished the various offices for monks, Daoists, and others. According to the *Basic Annals of Renzong* in the *History of Yuan*:
on the gengyin day of the third month of spring in the fourth year of Zhida, the Emperor ascended the throne;

in the fourth month of summer, he abolished the offices for monks, Daoists, Yeliqewen, Dashi-man, Tudu, and the Baiyunzong. According to the biography of Li Meng: Meng’s courtesy name was... [text truncated]
Dào Fù was appointed as the Grand Councilor (Zhōngshū Píngzhāng Zhèngshì) by Emperor Rénzōng upon his succession to the throne, and his rank was advanced to Guānglù Dàfū.

At that time, the two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism had established official offices for their governance; these officials wielded power rivaling that of the regular civil administration, thereby disrupting state affairs.

The monastics and Daoists were particularly distressed by this interference. Mèng remarked that the sovereign’s authority lies in reward and punishment: by rewarding a single act of goodness, the whole world is encouraged to follow suit.

"Punishing one evil person so that the whole world is deterred—this is how the handle of authority is not lost in its application. If the application is improper, there will be nothing to encourage or deter;
how then can there be governance? Since monks and Daoist priests have already entered the supramundane dharma, why should they be restrained and governed by the offices of the government?

He then memorialized to exonerate those who had died unjustly and restore their official ranks, to strip away the titles and honors of those who had obtained them through corruption and fraud, and to abolish the official positions for monks and Daoists. Heaven...
This was hailed with joy below.

In the seventh year of the Yanyou era of the Renzong reign, the Yingzong ascended the throne. The Censor-in-Chief requested that the excessive conferment of noble titles upon monks and Daoists be abolished.

According to the *Yuan Shi*, "Basic Annals of the Yingzong Reign": in the third month of spring in the seventh year of Yanyou, the Emperor ascended the throne; on the *renyin* day of the fifth month...
The Censor-in-Chief requested that the excessive bestowal of noble ranks upon monks and Daoists be abolished, as well as the expenditures for the construction of monasteries.
On the day of Bingwu, the Censor Liu Heng requested the establishment of public granaries and the confiscation of official titles held by monks and Daoists.

On the *xin-hai* day of the third month in the third year of the Zhizhi era of Emperor Yingzong, following the disturbances caused by Yuanming Wang Daoming, the issuance of monastic certificates (*du-chie*) for monks and nuns and talismanic registers (*fu-lu*) for Daoists was prohibited.
(As recorded in the *Basic Annals of Emperor Yingzong* in the *History of Yuan*, etc.)
In the first year of the Taiding era of Emperor Taiding, Zhang Gui and others submitted a petition requesting the reduction and abolition of sacrificial rites and Buddhist ceremonies.

They further proposed that monks and Daoists who had purchased private land should be made subject to corvée labor; those among them who kept wives and children were to be dismissed from their status and returned to the common people. [The Emperor] did not comply. (Note:
This is not recorded in the *Basic Annals* of Emperor Taiding in the *History of Yuan*. According to the biography of Zhang Gui, it occurred in the sixth month of the first year of the Taiding era.)
The imperial carriage was at the Upper Capital. Previously, the Emperor, due to portents and anomalies, had issued an edict for the various officials to assemble and deliberate.
Guī, together with officials from the Bureau of Military Affairs, the Censorate, and the two academies of the Hanlin and Jixian, vigorously discussed the merits and defects of the current age.

Accompanied by Song Wenzan, an Extraordinary Secretary of the Left and Right Bureaus, he traveled to the Upper Capital to present their memorial. Their proposal stated: "For successive reigns, the *wo'er*..."
The Changqiu, Chenghui, and Changning Temples established by Duosuo shall be dealt with separately from the military garrisons of the frontier regions.
Since ancient times, sagacious rulers have relied solely on sincerity in their governance; this alone can move Heaven and Earth and stir the ghosts and spirits.

From the beginning, they never sought blessings from monks or Daoists to oppress the people or bring disease upon the state. Furthermore, taking the year 30 of the Zhizhi era as an example regarding the *jiao* ritual:

Imperial Collected Works from the Fiftieth Year of the Kangxi Era.
On the fifteenth day of the twelfth month of the fiftieth year of the Kangxi era, the Emperor issued an edict to the Ministry of Rites:

"Recently, I have observed that there are a great many instances throughout the directly administered provinces and other regions where new temples and monasteries are being constructed. Regarding the building of these temples...
As for temples, they encroach upon the fields and dwellings of the common people.

Once completed, ignorant folk further provide for the daily needs of monks and Daoists by purchasing silver and money to grant them the lands of the poor; thus, the people's fields gradually diminish.
Moreover, vagrants fill the ranks of monks and Daoists, providing cover for fugitives and criminals to carry out their deeds.
The practitioners of the Dharma are exceedingly numerous; they truly disturb the localities and are of no great benefit to the livelihood of the people.

It is hereby decreed that all Provincial Governors, Circuit Intendants, and local officials shall, with the exception of existing temples, permanently prohibit the construction of new ones or the expansion and repair of those already standing.
(Tu Shu Ji Cheng) Shen Yi Dian, Section on the Two Schools, Comprehensive Examination, Volume Lower (End).
